Internship & Job Posting Click Analysis

Knowlton Center — Spring 2026

Marketing Analytics

2026-10-21

Executive Summary

This project evaluates student engagement with internship and job postings in the Knowlton Center’s Spring 2026 career newsletters to identify opportunities to improve content selection, placement, and presentation.

I found that featured postings generally attract more clicks, with engagement declining most noticeably after the first five positions. Employer recognition influences clicks in select communities, while shorter descriptions perform significantly better only in Exploration community. Based on these findings, I recommend prioritizing high-value postings in the top positions, expanding featured postings where effective, and tailoring content strategies to each career community rather than applying a uniform approach.

I analyzed clicks per posting across seven career communities using descriptive statistics and negative binomial regression. I examined four primary factors: featured status, posting position, employer recognition, and description length, while controlling for other relevant posting characteristics to better isolate their associations with engagement.

The regression model (one specification, used everywhere)

Clicks are counts and are over-dispersed (a few postings get many clicks, most get few), so we use negative binomial regression — glm.nb() from the MASS package. For each community we fit one model with the same four inputs:

\[\log(\text{expected clicks}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{featured} + \beta_2\,\text{rank\_in\_section} + \beta_3\,\text{is\_job} + \beta_4\,\text{recognition}\]

Each of our questions just reads a different coefficient out of this same model, while the other three act as controls:

Question Coefficient reported What the others do
Q1 Does featuring help? \(\beta_1\) (featured) hold position, section, recognition constant
Q2 Does position matter? \(\beta_2\) (rank) hold featuring, section, recognition constant
Q3 Does recognition matter? \(\beta_4\) (recognition) hold featuring, position, section constant
Q4 Does blurb length matter? adds \(\beta_5\) (words), featured-only —

We report each coefficient as an IRR (incidence rate ratio) = exp(β). An IRR of 1.42 means +42% clicks. Controlling for a variable means “comparing postings that are otherwise similar on it” — e.g. the featured effect is measured among postings at comparable positions, sections, and recognition levels.

Why control for all four, not just position? A raw comparison can be misleading if the groups differ on something else. The clearest example is SIEG (Q1): zero of its featured postings are high-recognition employers, but 27% of its non-featured ones are. So a raw “featured vs not” gap in SIEG partly measures “lesser-known employers,” not featuring. Controlling for recognition separates the two. We show both the raw and controlled numbers so this is visible.

# ---- Packages ------------------------------------------------------------
# tidyverse : dplyr (data wrangling) + ggplot2 (charts) + purrr (map_dfr)
# MASS      : glm.nb(), the negative binomial regression
# emmeans   : compares blurb-length groups after a model is fit
# broom     : tidy() turns a model's output into a neat data frame
library(tidyverse)
library(MASS)
library(emmeans)
library(broom)

# MASS also has a select(); force dplyr's version so our pipes work.
select <- dplyr::select

# ---- House style: Knowlton red ------------------------------------------
knowlton_red  <- "#C8102D"
knowlton_grey <- "#63666A"

theme_knowlton <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", color = knowlton_grey),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(color = knowlton_grey),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", color = knowlton_grey)
    )
}
# ---- Load both source files ---------------------------------------------
data        <- read.csv("spring26_featured_all.csv")
comp_lookup <- read.csv("company_lookup.csv")

# Keep only lookup rows that actually carry a recognition label,
# then attach that label to each posting by company name.
comp_lookup <- comp_lookup %>%
  filter(!is.na(recognition), recognition != "") %>%
  select(company, recognition) %>%
  distinct(company, .keep_all = TRUE)

data <- data %>% left_join(comp_lookup, by = "company")

# ---- Build the modelling variables --------------------------------------
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    # section_position is the posting's rank INSIDE its own section
    # (it restarts at 1 for the job section). This is the position we want:
    # "how many postings sit above me within my section".
    rank_in_section = section_position,

    is_job      = as.integer(section == "job"),           # 1 = job, 0 = internship
    featured    = factor(featured, levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    # "Low" is listed first so the model treats it as the baseline that
    # "High" is compared against.
    recognition = factor(recognition, levels = c("Low", "High"))
  )

# ---- TDS scraping fix -----------------------------------------------------
# Some TDS postings appear under a "Featured Internship" header but carry no
# blurb text; in the data they show up as featured with blurb_ct == 1. We
# verified these are effectively plain links, so we RECODE them to unfeatured
# with blurb_ct = 0 (the 4/8/9-word TDS blurbs are real and are left alone).
# One condition must change TWO columns, so we build a flag first, use it for
# both, then drop it.
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    tds_header_only = (cc == "TDS" & featured == "Yes" & blurb_ct == 1),
    featured = factor(if_else(tds_header_only, "No", as.character(featured)),
                      levels = c("No", "Yes")),
    blurb_ct = if_else(tds_header_only, 0L, blurb_ct)
  ) %>%
  select(-tds_header_only)

communities   <- c("EXPLORATION", "FCB", "HCRW", "MSC", "SIEG", "TDS", "VWPA")
featured_only <- data %>% filter(featured == "Yes")

0. Summary statistics (sample sizes behind the models)

Before any modelling, here is how much data sits in each bucket. These counts explain how much to trust each coefficient later: a lift estimated from 12 featured postings (MSC) has a much wider margin of error than one from 400+.

# Number of postings per community, split by featured status.
# pivot_wider turns the long counts into a compact cc-by-column table.
data %>%
  count(cc, featured) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = featured, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  rename(Featured = Yes, `Not featured` = No) %>%
  mutate(Total = Featured + `Not featured`)
# Postings per community split by section (internship vs job).
data %>%
  count(cc, section) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = section, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(Total = internship + job)
# Postings per community split by employer recognition.
# NA = company had no recognition label; those rows drop out of any model
# that includes recognition, so it's useful to see how many there are.
data %>%
  mutate(recognition = as.character(recognition),
         recognition = if_else(is.na(recognition), "No label", recognition)) %>%
  count(cc, recognition) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = recognition, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
# The key cross-tab for Q1: recognition split WITHIN featured vs not.
# This is what exposes the SIEG confound (0 high-recognition featured postings).
data %>%
  filter(!is.na(recognition)) %>%
  count(cc, featured, recognition) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(featured, recognition),
              values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
# Section length = number of postings in one section of one weekly email.
# We summarise its median / min / max / count per community, split two ways:
# (a) featured vs not, (b) internship vs job. This tells us how deep sections
# run -- which matters for reading the position/attention results (Section 2).

# First, compute the length of every (cc, week, section) block:
section_lengths <- data %>%
  group_by(cc, week, section) %>%
  summarise(sec_len = n(), .groups = "drop")

# (a) overall section length per community
section_lengths %>%
  group_by(cc) %>%
  summarise(median_len = median(sec_len), min_len = min(sec_len),
            max_len = max(sec_len), n_sections = n(), .groups = "drop")
# (b) same, split by section type (internship vs job)
section_lengths %>%
  group_by(cc, section) %>%
  summarise(median_len = median(sec_len), min_len = min(sec_len),
            max_len = max(sec_len), n_sections = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = section,
              values_from = c(median_len, min_len, max_len, n_sections),
              values_fill = 0)

Reading these: EXPLORATION and HCRW are ~100% featured (no non-featured group, so featuring can’t be tested there). MSC has only 12 featured postings — its lift will have a wide margin. SIEG has zero high-recognition featured postings, which is the confound Q1 has to handle. HCRW sections are short (median 4 postings), which is why its attention curve can’t run deep (Section 2).

The model helpers (read once, used by every question)

These two small functions save us from copy-pasting the same modelling code in every section. Heavily commented because they do the real work.

# build_cc_model() fits our one negative-binomial model for a single community.
#
# The catch: some controls have only ONE value inside a given community, and a
# regression cannot estimate a coefficient for a constant. Examples:
#   - EXPLORATION has internships only -> is_job is always 0 -> must be dropped
#   - a featured-only subset where every employer is Low recognition -> drop it
# If we left such a term in, glm.nb() would error and stop the whole report.
# So this function checks each control for variation and keeps only the usable
# ones. It returns BOTH the fitted model and the list of terms actually used.

build_cc_model <- function(df,
                           outcome  = "clicks",
                           focus    = "featured",            # the term we care about
                           controls = c("rank_in_section", "is_job", "recognition")) {

  # Step 1: keep only controls that vary in THIS community's data.
  usable_controls <- controls[map_lgl(controls, function(term) {
    # n_distinct counts unique values; na.rm ignores missing recognition labels.
    n_distinct(df[[term]], na.rm = TRUE) > 1
  })]

  # Step 2: if recognition is one of the controls, drop rows with no label
  # (otherwise glm.nb silently refuses to run).
  if ("recognition" %in% usable_controls) {
    df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(recognition))
  }

  # Step 3: build the formula string, e.g. "clicks ~ featured + rank_in_section"
  rhs     <- paste(c(focus, usable_controls), collapse = " + ")
  formula <- as.formula(paste(outcome, "~", rhs))

  # Step 4: fit safely. tryCatch returns NULL instead of crashing if the model
  # fails to converge (can happen in very small samples).
  model <- tryCatch(glm.nb(formula, data = df), error = function(e) NULL)

  # Return the model, the terms we used, and the row count behind it.
  list(model = model, terms_used = usable_controls, n = nrow(df))
}
# get_effect() pulls ONE coefficient out of a fitted model and turns it into a
# readable "+42%" style number.
#
#   exp(estimate)        -> IRR (incidence rate ratio)
#   (IRR - 1) * 100      -> percent change in clicks
#   p.value              -> significance, which we translate into stars
#
# Returns a one-row tibble, or NULL if the model/term isn't there.

get_effect <- function(model, term) {
  if (is.null(model)) return(NULL)

  tidy_model <- broom::tidy(model)          # model output as a data frame
  if (!term %in% tidy_model$term) return(NULL)

  row <- tidy_model %>% filter(term == !!term)

  tibble(
    IRR        = exp(row$estimate),
    pct_change = (exp(row$estimate) - 1) * 100,
    p_value    = row$p.value,
    sig        = case_when(               # standard significance stars
      row$p.value < .001 ~ "***",
      row$p.value < .01  ~ "**",
      row$p.value < .05  ~ "*",
      row$p.value < .10  ~ ".",
      TRUE               ~ "ns"
    )
  )
}

How map_dfr() is used below: map_dfr(communities, f) runs the function f once for each community and stacks the one-row results into a single table — it’s a clean “loop over communities and bind the rows” in one line.

# Quick pipeline check: a pooled model (all communities, cc as a control)
# should give featured IRR ~ 1.69, position-per-slot IRR ~ 0.975, job IRR ~ 0.53.
# The 1.69 (not 1.67) reflects the TDS recode moving 14 rows to unfeatured.
sanity <- glm.nb(clicks ~ featured + rank_in_section + is_job + recognition + cc,
                 data = data %>% filter(!is.na(recognition)))
round(exp(coef(sanity))[c("featuredYes", "rank_in_section", "is_job")], 3)
##     featuredYes rank_in_section          is_job 
##           1.685           0.975           0.532

1. Does featuring increase clicks? (by community)

We report \(\beta_1\) (featured) from the full model. Two communities can’t be tested — EXPLORATION (102/103 featured) and HCRW (111/112) — because there’s no non-featured group to compare against.

We show two numbers per community: the raw lift (position + section controls only) and the controlled lift (also controlling for recognition). Where they diverge, recognition was confounding the raw comparison.

featured_results <- map_dfr(communities, function(this_cc) {
  d_cc  <- data %>% filter(cc == this_cc)
  n_yes <- sum(d_cc$featured == "Yes")
  n_no  <- sum(d_cc$featured == "No")

  # Need enough of BOTH groups to compare.
  if (min(n_yes, n_no) < 10) {
    return(tibble(cc = this_cc, n_featured = n_yes, n_unfeatured = n_no,
                  raw_pct = NA, raw_sig = "not estimable",
                  controlled_pct = NA, controlled_sig = "not estimable"))
  }

  # RAW model: featured effect controlling only for position (+ section if present).
  raw_fit <- build_cc_model(d_cc, focus = "featured",
                            controls = c("rank_in_section", "is_job"))
  raw_eff <- get_effect(raw_fit$model, "featuredYes")

  # CONTROLLED model: add recognition to the controls.
  ctl_fit <- build_cc_model(d_cc, focus = "featured",
                            controls = c("rank_in_section", "is_job", "recognition"))
  ctl_eff <- get_effect(ctl_fit$model, "featuredYes")

  tibble(
    cc = this_cc, n_featured = n_yes, n_unfeatured = n_no,
    raw_pct        = round(raw_eff$pct_change, 0), raw_sig = raw_eff$sig,
    controlled_pct = round(ctl_eff$pct_change, 0), controlled_sig = ctl_eff$sig
  )
})

featured_results
# Plot the CONTROLLED lift for the communities we could estimate.
plot_df <- featured_results %>% filter(!is.na(controlled_pct))

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = reorder(cc, controlled_pct), y = controlled_pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = knowlton_red, width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(controlled_pct, "% ", controlled_sig)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 4, color = knowlton_grey) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  labs(title = "Featured lift by community (controlled for recognition)",
       subtitle = "% more clicks for featured vs. non-featured\n*** p<.001  ** p<.01  * p<.05  . p<.10  ns = not significant",
       x = NULL, y = "% change in clicks from featuring") +
  theme_knowlton()

How to read it. Featuring works in MSC (+113%), TDS (+106%), FCB (+89%), and is marginal in VWPA (+46%, p≈0.08) — and for these four, controlling for recognition barely moves the raw number, so the effect is real.

SIEG is the exception and the headline. Its raw lift (+42%, p=0.011) collapses to −9% (ns) once recognition is controlled. Because none of SIEG’s featured postings are high-recognition employers (see the cross-tab in Section 0), the raw “featured” gap was really measuring employer profile, not featuring. SIEG’s apparent featured benefit does not survive a basic control.

2. Position: how far down do students engage?

Marginal-click table. For every position (pooled across all communities), the average clicks and the number of postings at that position. This is the direct evidence for “attention falls off near the top.” We pool communities (no per-cc split) so each row has enough data to be stable.

marginal_table <- data %>%
  mutate(
    # Group deep positions together so the tail isn't a long list of tiny rows.
    position_bucket = if_else(rank_in_section >= 13, 13L, rank_in_section)
  ) %>%
  group_by(position_bucket) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_clicks   = round(mean(clicks), 2),
    n_postings    = n(),
    n_communities = n_distinct(cc),        # how many cc's still have a posting this deep
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(position = if_else(position_bucket == 13, "13+", as.character(position_bucket))) %>%
  select(position, mean_clicks, n_postings, n_communities)

marginal_table

Note on short-section communities. Every community contributes through slot 9. From slot 10 on, only 4–5 communities remain — HCRW (median section length 4), EXPLORATION (7) and TDS (9) simply run out of postings, so the deep rows are FCB / MSC / SIEG / VWPA. We keep them in the pooled numbers; just know the tail is driven by the longer-section communities.

# Visual version of the table above.
plot_marg <- data %>%
  filter(rank_in_section <= 20) %>%
  group_by(rank_in_section) %>%
  summarise(mean_clicks = mean(clicks), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n >= 3)                       # hide positions with too little data

ggplot(plot_marg, aes(rank_in_section, mean_clicks)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 8, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70") +
  geom_line(color = knowlton_red, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = knowlton_red, size = 1.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, 20, 2)) +
  labs(title = "Clicks fall through the first few slots, then flatten",
       subtitle = "Average clicks by position within a section (dashed line = slot 8)",
       x = "Position within section", y = "Average clicks") +
  theme_knowlton()

By cc

# Average clicks by position within a section, per community.
# ONE line (all postings). We trim ranks with too few postings so the noisy
# deep tail (where late spikes are just 1-2 postings) doesn't mislead.
curve_df <- data %>%
  group_by(cc, rank_in_section) %>%
  summarise(mean_clicks = mean(clicks), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n >= 15)                     # keep only well-supported positions

ggplot(curve_df, aes(rank_in_section, mean_clicks)) +
  # shade the first 5 slots: "where ordering matters"
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.5, xmax = 5.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = knowlton_red, alpha = 0.06) +
  # smoothed trend (light) under the actual points/line
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, span = 0.9, color = knowlton_grey,
              linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "22") +
  geom_line(color = knowlton_red, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(color = knowlton_red, size = 1.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ cc, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 25, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Clicks fall through the first few slots, then flatten",
       subtitle = "Average clicks by position within a section  •  shaded = first 5 slots (where ordering matters)  •  positions with <15 postings dropped",
       x = "Position within section", y = "Average clicks") +
  theme_knowlton() +
  theme(panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"))

The per-slot model. For a single-number summary, the pooled position coefficient (full controls) is −2.5% per slot (p < 0.001): each step down costs about 2–3% of clicks. Consistent with the table — steep at the top, negligible past slot ~8.

pos_model <- glm.nb(clicks ~ featured + rank_in_section + is_job + recognition + cc,
                    data = data %>% filter(!is.na(recognition)))
get_effect(pos_model, "rank_in_section")

Does a longer section dilute the top postings? No. We model the clicks of the top-3 postings against section length: if longer sections stole attention from the top, this would be negative. It isn’t in any community.

top3 <- data %>%
  group_by(cc, week, section) %>%
  mutate(sec_len = n()) %>%          # length of this posting's section
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(rank_in_section <= 3)       # keep only the top 3 of each section

dilution_results <- map_dfr(communities, function(this_cc) {
  d_cc <- top3 %>% filter(cc == this_cc)

  # Need enough rows and enough different section lengths to estimate a slope.
  if (nrow(d_cc) < 25 || n_distinct(d_cc$sec_len) < 3) {
    return(tibble(cc = this_cc, pct_per_extra_posting = NA,
                  p_value = NA, sig = "thin data"))
  }

  fit <- build_cc_model(d_cc, focus = "sec_len",
                        controls = c("rank_in_section", "is_job", "recognition"))
  eff <- get_effect(fit$model, "sec_len")
  if (is.null(eff)) return(tibble(cc = this_cc, pct_per_extra_posting = NA,
                                  p_value = NA, sig = "fit failed"))

  tibble(cc = this_cc,
         pct_per_extra_posting = round(eff$pct_change, 1),
         p_value = round(eff$p_value, 3), sig = eff$sig)
})

dilution_results

Interpretation (your framing, confirmed): ordering matters in roughly the first 4–5 slots and is essentially flat by slot ~8. Adding postings deeper does not cost the top postings clicks — no community shows negative dilution (FCB is even slightly positive). So a longer section is close to free: late postings earn a little and take nothing from the top. Caveat: we can’t fully separate “students stop scrolling” from “editors place better postings up top,” so we describe where engagement drops, not why.

3. Does employer recognition influence clicks? (by community)

We report \(\beta_4\) (recognition) from the full model — the effect of a high-recognition employer vs. a low one, holding featuring, position, and section constant.

recognition_results <- map_dfr(communities, function(this_cc) {
  d_cc <- data %>% filter(cc == this_cc, !is.na(recognition))

  n_high <- sum(d_cc$recognition == "High")
  n_low  <- sum(d_cc$recognition == "Low")
  if (min(n_high, n_low) < 10) {
    return(tibble(cc = this_cc, n_high = n_high, n_low = n_low,
                  pct_change = NA, p_value = NA, sig = "not estimable"))
  }

  # recognition is the focus here; featured/position/section are controls.
  fit <- build_cc_model(d_cc, focus = "recognition",
                        controls = c("featured", "rank_in_section", "is_job"))
  eff <- get_effect(fit$model, "recognitionHigh")
  if (is.null(eff)) return(tibble(cc = this_cc, n_high = n_high, n_low = n_low,
                                  pct_change = NA, p_value = NA, sig = "fit failed"))

  tibble(cc = this_cc, n_high = n_high, n_low = n_low,
         pct_change = round(eff$pct_change, 0),
         p_value = round(eff$p_value, 4), sig = eff$sig)
})

recognition_results %>% arrange(desc(pct_change))

Reading it. Recognition helps clearly in HCRW (+47%, p=0.04) and directionally in EXPLORATION (+54%, p≈0.09) and VWPA (+28%, p≈0.06). Elsewhere it’s not significant. There is no community where high-recognition employers resist being placed lower, so we should not claim “put big names at the bottom.” Note this is the effect across all postings; recognition is not a reliable lever inside the featured slots specifically.

4. Does blurb length matter? (featured postings only)

Blurb length only exists for featured postings, so this is featured-only. We add a blurb-count term to the model. Two views: continuous (per 10 words) and Short/Medium/Long groups.

# Split each community's featured postings into three length groups and show
# what those groups mean (word ranges) plus average clicks.
tertile_data <- featured_only %>%
  filter(!is.na(blurb_ct)) %>%
  group_by(cc) %>%
  filter(n() >= 15) %>%                       # only communities with enough data
  mutate(length_group = cut(
    blurb_ct,
    breaks = quantile(blurb_ct, probs = c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1)),  # cut at the thirds
    labels = c("Short", "Medium", "Long"),
    include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

tertile_data %>%
  group_by(cc, length_group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), min_words = min(blurb_ct), median_words = median(blurb_ct),
            max_words = max(blurb_ct), mean_clicks = round(mean(clicks), 1),
            .groups = "drop")
blurb_results <- map_dfr(communities, function(this_cc) {
  d_cc <- featured_only %>% filter(cc == this_cc, !is.na(blurb_ct))
  if (nrow(d_cc) < 15) {
    return(tibble(cc = this_cc, n = nrow(d_cc), median_words = NA,
                  pct_per_10_words = NA, p_value = NA, sig = "n too small"))
  }

  # Focus is blurb_ct; recognition/position/section are controls (featured is
  # constant here, so build_cc_model will automatically drop it).
  fit <- build_cc_model(d_cc, focus = "blurb_ct",
                        controls = c("rank_in_section", "is_job", "recognition"))
  eff <- get_effect(fit$model, "blurb_ct")
  if (is.null(eff)) return(tibble(cc = this_cc, n = nrow(d_cc), median_words = NA,
                                  pct_per_10_words = NA, p_value = NA, sig = "fit failed"))

  # The coefficient is per 1 word; compound it to a per-10-word change so the
  # number is readable.
  per10 <- (eff$IRR^10 - 1) * 100
  tibble(cc = this_cc, n = nrow(d_cc),
         median_words = median(d_cc$blurb_ct),
         pct_per_10_words = round(per10, 1),
         p_value = round(eff$p_value, 4), sig = eff$sig)
})

blurb_results
# ---- Helper: format p-values as readable floats ---------------------------
# Very small p-values print as "3.3e-11" by default, which is unreadable.
# This shows "<0.001" for tiny values, otherwise a plain 3-decimal number
# (e.g. 0.033). Keeps the raw numeric p-value too, for sorting/filtering.
format_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
}

# ---- Pairwise blurb-length comparisons, per community ---------------------
# For each community with all three length groups, fit the model (controlling
# for position) and use emmeans + pairs() to compare the groups. pairs() with
# type = "response" returns each comparison as a RATIO of clicks
# (e.g. Short / Medium = 1.81 means Short gets 81% more clicks than Medium).
blurb_pairs <- tertile_data %>%
  group_by(cc) %>%
  group_modify(function(d_cc, key) {
    if (n_distinct(d_cc$length_group) < 2) return(tibble())
    m <- tryCatch(glm.nb(clicks ~ length_group + rank_in_section, data = d_cc),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(m)) return(tibble())
    emmeans(m, ~ length_group, type = "response") %>%
      pairs(adjust = "tukey") %>%
      as.data.frame()
  }) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Build the presentable columns:
  transmute(
    Community   = cc,
    Comparison  = gsub("/", "vs", contrast),          # "Short / Medium" -> "Short vs Medium"
    `% difference` = round((ratio - 1) * 100, 0),      # +81 means first group gets 81% more
    ratio       = round(ratio, 2),
    p_value     = round(p.value, 4),                   # raw numeric, for reference
    `p (formatted)` = format_p(p.value),               # readable: "<0.001" or "0.033"
    Significant = if_else(p.value < 0.05, "Yes", "no")
  ) %>%
  arrange(Community, desc(`% difference`))

# Clean table for the report
knitr::kable(blurb_pairs, align = "llrrrrc",
             caption = "Blurb-length comparisons within each community (featured postings). % difference = how many more clicks the first group gets than the second.")

# EXPLORATION is the standout: short blurbs win big.
expl <- tertile_data %>%
  filter(cc == "EXPLORATION") %>%
  group_by(length_group) %>%
  summarise(mean_clicks = mean(clicks), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(expl, aes(length_group, mean_clicks)) +
  geom_col(fill = knowlton_red, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_clicks, 1)), vjust = -0.4,
            size = 4.5, color = knowlton_grey) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "EXPLORATION: short blurbs win by a wide margin",
       subtitle = "Average clicks by blurb-length group (featured postings)",
       x = "Blurb length group", y = "Average clicks") +
  theme_knowlton()

Takeaway. Blurb length clearly matters only in EXPLORATION, where short blurbs (median ~33 words) get several times the clicks of longer ones — large and robust. Elsewhere the direction is mixed and non-significant, so “shorter is better” is an EXPLORATION rule, not a house rule.

5. Internship vs. job, within each community (informational)

These serve different audiences (younger students vs. seniors) and are unevenly represented, so this is context, not a recommendation to drop jobs. It just shows where the two behave differently. We report \(\beta_3\) (is_job).

int_job_results <- map_dfr(communities, function(this_cc) {
  d_cc <- data %>% filter(cc == this_cc)
  if (n_distinct(d_cc$section) < 2) {
    return(tibble(cc = this_cc, n_job = 0, n_internship = nrow(d_cc),
                  pct_job_vs_internship = NA, p_value = NA, sig = "internship only"))
  }

  # is_job is the focus; featured/position/recognition are controls.
  fit <- build_cc_model(d_cc, focus = "is_job",
                        controls = c("featured", "rank_in_section", "recognition"))
  eff <- get_effect(fit$model, "is_job")

  tibble(cc = this_cc,
         n_job = sum(d_cc$section == "job"),
         n_internship = sum(d_cc$section == "internship"),
         pct_job_vs_internship = round(eff$pct_change, 0),
         p_value = round(eff$p_value, 5), sig = eff$sig)
})

int_job_results

Takeaway. In most communities job postings get fewer clicks than internships — expected, given different audiences. The useful exception is MSC, where jobs and internships perform about the same. MSC is the one community where a full-time role is worth the same placement effort as an internship.

Summary of findings

Question Finding
Featuring works? Yes: MSC (+113%), TDS (+106%), FCB (+89%); marginal VWPA (+46%). SIEG’s raw +42% vanishes to -9% once recognition is controlled. EXPLORATION & HCRW ~all featured (can’t test).
Position matters? Yes - clicks drop through the first ~5 slots, flat by ~slot 8 (~-2.5%/slot).
Section length hurts top? No - adding deeper postings does not reduce clicks to the top 3.
Recognition matters? Clearly in HCRW (+47%); directional in EXPLORATION (+54%) and VWPA (+28%).
Blurb length matters? Only in EXPLORATION (short wins big). Not a general rule.
Jobs vs internships Jobs get fewer clicks except in MSC, where they match internships.

Recommendations (for the marketing manager)

Per community

  • MSC — Featuring pays off most (+113%) but only 12 slots were used all semester. Biggest single opportunity: feature more in MSC. Jobs match internships here, so treat them equally.
  • FCB — Featuring works (+89%). Recognition doesn’t move clicks, so don’t chase brand names; put the effort into placement.
  • TDS — Featuring works (+106%, measured on real-blurb postings after the scraping recode). Fix the blurb scraping so length can be evaluated cleanly.
  • SIEG — The apparent featured lift is an artifact of which employers get featured (all lesser-known); it disappears once recognition is controlled. Before spending more featured effort here, look at what’s being featured.
  • HCRW — Short sections, so ordering matters most at the very top. Recognizable employers do better (+47%).
  • VWPA — Lowest engagement overall; recognizable employers help (+28%).
  • EXPLORATION — Keep featured blurbs short (~35 words). Strongest, most actionable single finding.

Across all communities

  1. Order the top of each section deliberately. The first ~5 slots carry almost all of the position effect; below slot ~8 it barely matters.
  2. Don’t fear long sections. Extra postings add clicks and don’t steal from the top — a longer newsletter is close to free.
  3. Featuring is a real lever where it can be tested — but always check what’s being featured. SIEG shows how a raw lift can be an employer-mix effect in disguise.
